Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1








NoteWhat is a regression, in one paragraph?



A regression estimates how much an outcome changes when something else changes. Here the outcome is “the share of a student’s text that belongs to topic k,” and the “something else” is whether the student is a graduate student. The answer is a coefficient: the difference in that share between the groups. A standard error says how uncertain that difference is. A rough rule is that a coefficient more than about two standard errors from zero is unlikely to be pure chance.




1:K ~ level is the formula: “for topics 1 through K, relate the topic share to level.”

metadata = out$meta supplies the covariates.

summary(effect, topics = 1:3) prints the results for the first three topics.

Each topic’s results have an intercept (the expected topic share for undergraduates, the reference group) and a levelGraduate coefficient (how much higher or lower graduate students are). A coefficient of 0.03 means graduate students devote 3 percentage points more of their answers to that topic. Look at the Estimate, the Std. Error, and the p-value column. The p-value is the chance of seeing a difference this big if there were really none; small values (conventionally under 0.05) suggest a real difference.
Here is what the first three topics showed. Topics 1 and 3 have coefficients near zero (0.001 and -0.004) with large p-values (0.95 and 0.79): no evidence of a difference. Topic 2 stands out. Graduate students are estimated to use it about 4 percentage points more (0.041, p = 0.002), which looks like a clear finding. The plot below shows all eight topics, and a second topic turns out to stand out too.






WarningA false alarm, by construction



In the synthetic data, student level was assigned at random, so there is no real difference between graduate and undergraduate students to find. A “significant” result for topic 2 (and, as the plot below shows, a borderline one for topic 8) is therefore a false alarm. This is exactly what the next warning predicts: when you test eight topics at once, something will occasionally look significant by chance. It is also the best argument for the habit this book keeps repeating. Before believing a topic-by-group difference, read the documents behind it, and ask whether the story makes sense and whether it would hold up in a different sample.


Rather than read eight regression tables, plot the differences.

plot(effect,
     covariate  = "level",
     topics     = 1:K,
     model      = fit,
     method     = "difference",
     cov.value1 = "Graduate",
     cov.value2 = "Undergraduate",
     xlab       = "More undergraduate  <---->  More graduate",
     labeltype  = "custom",
     custom.labels = paste("Topic", 1:K),
     verbose.labels = FALSE)






Figure 5.2: Difference in topic proportion, Graduate minus Undergraduate. Intervals that cross zero are not distinguishable from no difference.




The options explained:


covariate = "level" says which characteristic we are comparing on.

method = "difference" plots the difference between two groups. cov.value1 = "Graduate" and cov.value2 = "Undergraduate" say which two, and the difference is the first minus the second. So a dot to the right of zero means graduate students use the topic more.

model = fit supplies the fitted model (needed for labels).

xlab sets the label of the horizontal axis. labeltype = "custom" with custom.labels lets us label each row “Topic 1,” “Topic 2,” and so on, instead of listing words. (paste("Topic", 1:K) builds those labels.)

Read this the way you read any effect estimate: look at the interval, the horizontal line through each dot, which shows the range of plausible differences. If the line crosses zero, the data are consistent with no difference at all. Most intervals will cross zero, because we have fewer than 200 graduate students. A topic whose interval clearly excludes zero is a candidate finding. Go back and read the graduate and undergraduate documents for that topic before saying anything about it.

5.7.1 Reading the chart from our run
Each row is a topic. The dot is the estimated difference in the share of a student’s text (graduate minus undergraduate), and the line is its 95% interval. The dashed vertical line marks zero, “no difference.” A dot to the right of it means graduate students use the topic more; to the left, undergraduates do. The whole horizontal range is small, from about -0.06 to +0.06, which means differences of at most a few percentage points.


Six of the eight lines cross zero. Topics 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, and 7 all have dots close to zero and lines that straddle it. For these there is no evidence of any difference. Topic 7’s dot is a little to the left (about -0.013) but its line is wide, so it is well within the noise.

Topic 2 sits to the right of zero. The dot is at about +0.04, and the whole line (roughly +0.015 to +0.065) is right of the dashed line. Taken at face value, graduate students use topic 2 more.

Topic 8 sits to the left of zero, barely. The dot is at about -0.03, and the line (roughly -0.065 to -0.002) only just stays on the left side of zero. Taken at face value, undergraduates use this topic more. Topic 8 is the note-taking-style topic from earlier, which is exactly the kind of result that tempts a story (“graduate students were interviewed differently”). A line that just clears zero deserves extra skepticism.

Both of those results are false alarms. Student level was assigned at random in this synthetic data, so there is nothing to find. Two of eight is a bit more than the roughly 0.4 you would expect by chance at the 5% level, but it is not out of the question, and it is a vivid illustration of why the “eight topics, eight tests” warning below matters. This chart looks like a finding. Reading the documents behind topics 2 and 8, and noticing that a plausible story is easy to invent, is what protects you from reporting it.
A note on the picture itself: the labels are drawn next to the dots, so a label may touch the dashed line (as “Topic 2” does). That is cosmetic and comes from the plotting function.






ImportantEight topics, eight tests



We are looking at eight differences at once. If there were no true differences, about one interval in twenty would still miss zero by chance, and with eight topics you should expect it to happen sometimes. (A standard remedy is to demand stronger evidence when you run many tests, for example by dividing the 0.05 cutoff by the number of tests.) Treat the topic-by-level comparisons as a way to generate hypotheses, and confirm anything interesting by reading and by a different sample if you can.

Look for

A K where the curve stops climbing

title: 6  Sentiment Analysis
text:
6.1 Sentiment lexicons
Data for this chapter: data/vcu_cares_long.csv
Sentiment analysis asks how positive or negative the language is. The simplest version is lexicon-based: take a dictionary that labels words as positive or negative, count the positive and negative words in each answer, and subtract. That is what we do here. It is transparent, it needs no training data, and it fails in instructive ways.
By the end of this chapter you will be able to score text with a sentiment lexicon, compare scores across groups, and, most importantly, check whether the scores mean what they appear to mean.
A lexicon is a word list with labels attached. A sentiment lexicon labels each word as positive or negative (or gives it a score). tidytext ships the Bing lexicon (Hu & Liu, 2004), which marks about 6,800 words as positive or negative.
bing <- get_sentiments("bing")
bing |> count(sentiment)

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  sentiment     n
  <chr>     <int>
1 negative   4781
2 positive   2005

head(bing, 8)

# A tibble: 8 × 2
  word        sentiment
  <chr>       <chr>    
1 2-faces     negative 
2 abnormal    negative 
3 abolish     negative 
4 abominable  negative 
5 abominably  negative 
6 abominate   negative 
7 abomination negative 
8 abort       negative
get_sentiments("bing") loads the lexicon as a table with two columns: word and sentiment. The second line counts how many words are labeled positive and how many negative, and head(bing, 8) shows the first eight rows. (The Bing lexicon has more negative words than positive ones, a common feature of English that matters when we compare scores.)
Two other lexicons are common.
AFINN and NRC are available through get_sentiments(), but they require the textdata package and a one-time download that asks you to accept a license, so we stick with Bing for reproducibility.

title: 6  Sentiment Analysis
text:
Lexicon
What it gives you



Bing
Each word is positive or negative


AFINN
Each word has a score from -5 (very negative) to +5 (very positive), so you get intensity



NRC
Each word is tagged with emotions such as trust, fear, anger, and joy

title: 6  Sentiment Analysis
text:
6.2 Scoring each answer
The steps: split the text into words, join the words to the lexicon, and count. Words that are not in the lexicon simply drop out.

tokens <- vcu |>
  unnest_tokens(word, text)

scores <- tokens |>
  inner_join(bing, by = "word") |>
  count(doc_id, sentiment) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = sentiment, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) |>
  mutate(net = positive - negative)

# Attach back to every answer; answers with no lexicon words score 0
vcu_sent <- vcu |>
  left_join(scores, by = "doc_id") |>
  mutate(across(c(positive, negative, net), \(x) replace_na(x, 0)),
         n_words = str_count(text, "\\S+"))

summary(vcu_sent$net)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
-6.0000  0.0000  1.0000  0.8843  2.0000 10.0000 

mean(vcu_sent$net == 0)

[1] 0.3097448


This block does two things: it scores the sentiment words, and then it attaches those scores back to the full list of answers.
Part 1: build the scores.


unnest_tokens(word, text) splits each answer into words, as in Chapter 2. Note that we do not remove stop words here: the lexicon ignores words it does not know, and some stop words (like “not”) matter for negation.

inner_join(bing, by = "word") matches each word to the lexicon. An inner join keeps only rows that have a match in both tables, so every word not in the lexicon disappears, and each remaining word gets a sentiment label.

count(doc_id, sentiment) counts, for each answer, how many positive and how many negative words it has.

pivot_wider(names_from = sentiment, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) reshapes the table so that positive and negative are separate columns. values_fill = 0 writes a zero where an answer has no words of one kind (without it, those cells would be blank).

mutate(net = positive - negative) creates the net sentiment score: positive words minus negative words. An answer with three positive words and one negative has a net score of +2.

Part 2: attach the scores to all answers.


left_join(scores, by = "doc_id") adds the score columns to every answer. A left join keeps every row of the first table (all of our answers) even if there is no match. Answers that contained no lexicon words have no row in scores, so they receive blanks (NA).

mutate(across(c(positive, negative, net), \(x) replace_na(x, 0))) fills those blanks with zeros. across() applies the same step to several columns at once, and replace_na(x, 0) replaces missing values with 0. The odd-looking \(x) ... is a small function written on the spot (“take x and replace its blanks with zeros”).

n_words = ... adds each answer’s word count, which we use later.

The last two lines summarize the net scores. summary() shows the range, median, and mean. mean(vcu_sent$net == 0) is a trick worth knowing: vcu_sent$net == 0 gives TRUE or FALSE for each answer, and the mean of a list of TRUEs and FALSEs is the share that are TRUE, so this reports the fraction of answers that scored exactly zero.
A large share of answers score exactly zero. Many are short, and many contain no word the lexicon knows. A zero here means “no signal,” not “neutral.”

title: 6  Sentiment Analysis
text:
6.3 Sentiment by question
The three questions were written to invite different feelings, so the first sanity check is whether the scores reflect that.

by_q <- vcu_sent |>
  group_by(question) |>
  summarise(mean = mean(net), se = sd(net) / sqrt(n()), n = n())

by_q

# A tibble: 3 × 4
  question    mean     se     n
  <fct>      <dbl>  <dbl> <int>
1 strength  1.92   0.0450  1227
2 concern  -0.0885 0.0424  1085
3 idea      0.690  0.0300  1136

ggplot(by_q, aes(question, mean)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean - 1.96 * se, ymax = mean + 1.96 * se), width = 0.2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.3) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Mean net sentiment (positive minus negative words)")






Figure 6.1: Mean net sentiment for each question. Error bars are 95% confidence intervals.




The summary table. For each question (group_by(question)), summarise() computes three numbers:


mean: the average net score.

se: the standard error, a measure of how uncertain that average is. It is calculated as the standard deviation (sd(), which measures how spread out the scores are) divided by the square root of the number of answers (sqrt(n()), where n() counts rows in the group). A bigger group gives a smaller standard error: more answers means a more precise average.

n: how many answers are in the group.

The chart. geom_col() draws a bar at each question’s mean. geom_errorbar() adds the whiskers: from mean - 1.96 * se to mean + 1.96 * se. This range is a 95% confidence interval, the span of values that plausibly contains the true average. (The number 1.96 comes from the normal distribution; it is the multiple of the standard error that covers 95%.) geom_hline(yintercept = 0) draws a thin line at zero for reference.
Strengths score clearly positive, and ideas land in between. Concerns are the surprise: their mean is close to zero (slightly below), not strongly negative. Answers to “what is your biggest concern?” contain nearly as many positive words as negative ones.
That sounds wrong until you read the answers. Students phrase concerns as wishes (“need better advising appointments,” “more support with registration would help”), and a lexicon sees “better,” “support,” and “helpful” and scores them positive. It cannot tell that the sentence is a complaint. This is the central limit of lexicon sentiment: it measures the vocabulary of positivity, not the stance of the speaker.






ImportantCompare within a question, not across them



A concern is supposed to be negative, so a negative score on a concern says little about how that student feels about VCU. The interesting comparisons are within a question: is one group’s concern more negative than another’s? We do that next.

title: 6  Sentiment Analysis
text:
6.4 Sentiment by student level

vcu_sent |>
  filter(level %in% c("Undergraduate", "Graduate")) |>
  group_by(question, level) |>
  summarise(mean = mean(net), se = sd(net) / sqrt(n()), n = n(), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(question, mean, fill = level)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.8), width = 0.7) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean - 1.96 * se, ymax = mean + 1.96 * se),
                position = position_dodge(width = 0.8), width = 0.2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Undergraduate = vcu_teal, Graduate = vcu_gold)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Mean net sentiment", fill = NULL)






Figure 6.2: Net sentiment by question and student level.




This is the same calculation, now for each combination of question and level (group_by(question, level)). The chart options are new:


fill = level colors the bars by level.

position = position_dodge(width = 0.8) places the two bars for each question side by side instead of stacking them. The error bars get the same position_dodge() so that they line up with their bars.

scale_fill_manual(values = c(...)) chooses the colors by hand: teal for undergraduates, gold for graduates.

.groups = "drop" ungroups the result after summarise().

Check whether the intervals for the two levels overlap within each question. Where they do, we cannot say the groups differ, and the gap between the bars is within noise. Resist reading a story into a difference smaller than its error bar.

title: 6  Sentiment Analysis
6  Sentiment Analysis
text:
6.6 Where lexicons fail: negation
Lexicons count words one at a time, so they cannot see “not good.” We can at least measure how often a sentiment word follows a negator (a word like “not” or “never” that flips the meaning).

negators <- c("not", "no", "never", "without", "don't", "doesn't", "isn't",
              "wasn't", "can't", "couldn't", "won't", "hardly")

bigram_sent <- vcu |>
  unnest_tokens(bigram, text, token = "ngrams", n = 2) |>
  filter(!is.na(bigram)) |>
  separate(bigram, c("w1", "w2"), sep = " ") |>
  filter(w1 %in% negators) |>
  inner_join(bing, by = c("w2" = "word"))

bigram_sent |> count(w1, w2, sentiment, sort = TRUE) |> head(10)

# A tibble: 3 × 4
  w1      w2         sentiment     n
  <chr>   <chr>      <chr>     <int>
1 not     enough     positive     52
2 not     accessible positive     49
3 doesn't like       positive     37

nrow(bigram_sent)

[1] 138

n_matches <- nrow(inner_join(tokens, bing, by = "word"))   # all sentiment-word matches, for scale



negators is a list we typed by hand of words that flip meaning.
The pipeline splits each answer into bigrams (pairs of neighboring words, as in Chapter 2), then splits each pair into a first word w1 and a second word w2.

filter(w1 %in% negators) keeps pairs where the first word is a negator.

inner_join(bing, by = c("w2" = "word")) looks up the second word of each pair in the lexicon. Because the column is called w2 in our table but word in the lexicon, we tell R how to match them with c("w2" = "word").
The result is every case of “negator + sentiment word,” such as “not enough.” We show the most common ten and count them all with nrow().
The last line counts all sentiment-word matches in the data, for scale.

Each of these is a case where Bing assigned the wrong sign. “Not enough” and “not accessible” are the biggest: “enough” and “accessible” are positive in the lexicon, but here they follow “not.” “Doesn’t like” is the same problem. Out of about 5,487 sentiment-word matches, 138 follow a negator, roughly 3%. So negation is not wrecking the averages here, but it would matter much more in longer, more argumentative text.
Note that fixing negation does not solve the concern problem above. Dropping “enough” from the lexicon barely moves the mean for concerns. The bigger issue is that concerns are worded with positive vocabulary.

title: 6  Sentiment Analysis
text:
6.7 Reading the extremes
As always, check the numbers against the text. Here are the most negative and most positive concerns:

vcu_sent |>
  filter(question == "concern", n_words >= 5) |>
  arrange(net) |>
  slice_head(n = 4) |>
  select(net, text)

# A tibble: 4 × 2
    net text                                                                    
  <int> <chr>                                                                   
1    -6 Too expensive: the overall experience. Problems with the chances to giv…
2    -5 Frustrated with the system. Unclear who to ask about the school spirit …
3    -5 Struggling with the graduation checks. Disappointed by the advising app…
4    -5 too expensive: the getting help when needed. Struggling with the late-n…

vcu_sent |>
  filter(question == "concern", n_words >= 5) |>
  arrange(desc(net)) |>
  slice_head(n = 4) |>
  select(net, text)

# A tibble: 4 × 2
    net text                                                                    
  <int> <chr>                                                                   
1     7 The communication are not accessible to everyone. A better support for …
2     5 The financial aid paperwork could be a lot better. A better how things …
3     5 Need better overall epxerience. Would be great to have more staff train…
4     5 Need better making friends. A better support for students would be good…


Each block keeps concern answers of at least five words (very short answers are not informative), sorts them by net score, and shows four. arrange(net) sorts from lowest to highest, so the first block shows the most negative answers; arrange(desc(net)) sorts from highest to lowest, so the second shows the most positive ones.
Read the most positive concerns and you will see that they are complaints worded with “better,” “support,” and “helpful.” Their high scores come from wish-phrasing and negation, not from happiness. This is the kind of result that looks fine in a chart and falls apart when you read it.
Length is a second distortion. Within the concerns, both positive and negative word counts rise with answer length (correlations around .6), so longer answers spread out to the extremes while short ones sit near zero. (A correlation measures how closely two quantities move together, from 0 for unrelated to 1 for perfectly in step.) You could divide by length or use the positive share instead of a raw difference. Neither is clearly right; it depends on whether you think a long complaint is “more negative” than a short one.

title: 6  Sentiment Analysis
text:
6.8 Summary

Lexicon sentiment is fast, transparent, and crude. The score is positive words minus negative words.
Compare within a question, not across questions that invite different feelings.
Always inspect the words driving a score. Topic words and function words carrying sentiment labels bias results.
Negation, sarcasm, and length all distort scores. The supervised methods in Chapter 7, or a language model, handle these better, at the cost of transparency.

title: 7  Supervised Learning: Predicting Topic Codes
text:
7.1 The idea of supervised learning
Data for this chapter: data/vcu_cares_long.csv
Everything so far has been unsupervised: we asked the computer to find patterns without telling it what to look for. In supervised learning we give it an answer key. The model learns to reproduce the key from the text, and then we test it on answers it has not seen.
Our answer key is the interviewers’ topic codes. For most strength and concern answers in the original form, the interviewer ticked which topics the student discussed (Advising, Dining, Safety, and so on). Can a model look only at the words and predict those ticks?
By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain how a supervised model is trained and tested, build a model that predicts a topic code from text, and judge it with the measures that matter (and avoid the one that misleads).
glmnet fits the model we use (a regularized regression, explained below). Matrix provides the efficient “sparse” matrices we build for it.
Think of how you would teach a new research assistant to code answers into topics. You would show them a stack of answers that have already been coded. They would notice patterns (“answers that mention dorm and rent are coded Housing”) and then try coding new answers on their own. To check how well they learned, you would give them answers they have not seen and compare their codes to the correct ones.
A supervised model does the same, with three pieces:
The held-back test data is the crucial piece. A model can always do well on data it has already seen, just by memorizing it. The only fair question is how it does on new answers.

title: 7  Supervised Learning: Predicting Topic Codes
text:
Training data: answers with known codes, which the model learns from.

Test data: answers with known codes that are held back, used only to grade the finished model.

Features: the numbers that describe each answer to the model. Here they will be TF-IDF scores for each word.
crumbs: 7  Supervised Learning: Predicting Topic Codes

title: 7  Supervised Learning: Predicting Topic Codes
text:
7.2 Why bother?
Hand-coding is slow. If a model can reproduce the codes reasonably well, it can code new batches of interviews, flag answers for a second human look, or show which words an interviewer was responding to. The value depends on how well, and “how well” has to be measured on data the model never saw.
crumbs: 7  Supervised Learning: Predicting Topic Codes

title: 7  Supervised Learning: Predicting Topic Codes
text:
7.3 Step 1: Build the labeled set
Only answers with at least one topic code can teach or test the model.

labeled <- vcu |>
  filter(!is.na(topics)) |>
  mutate(
    text_id = row_number(),
    topics = str_split(topics, ";\\s*")
  )

nrow(labeled)

[1] 1897




filter(!is.na(topics)) keeps answers that have a topic code (the ! means “not,” so “not missing”).

text_id = row_number() gives every kept answer a new ID, 1, 2, 3, and so on, which we will use to line up rows with matrix positions.

str_split(topics, ";\\s*") splits each answer’s codes, stored as a single string like “Advising; Safety,” into a list of separate codes ("Advising", "Safety"). The pattern ;\\s* means “a semicolon followed by any spaces.” The topics column now holds a list for each answer.

Each answer can have several codes, so this is a multi-label problem. The easiest way to handle that is to treat each topic as its own yes/no question: “Is this answer about Advising?” “Is it about Safety?” Let us see how common each topic is.

topic_counts <- labeled |>
  unnest(topics) |>
  count(topics, sort = TRUE) |>
  mutate(pct = n / nrow(labeled))

topic_counts |>
  ggplot(aes(n, reorder(topics, n))) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "Answers with this code", y = NULL)






Figure 7.1: How often each topic code was assigned.




unnest(topics) is the opposite of the splitting we just did: it turns each list of codes into separate rows, one per code, so we can count them. mutate(pct = ...) records each code’s share of all labeled answers.
Some topics are common (“Student activities”), and some are rare (“Staff development”). Rare topics will be hard to learn: with only a dozen examples, there is little for the model to generalize from. We start with one topic and then scale up.

target <- "Student activities"
labeled <- labeled |>
  mutate(y = map_lgl(topics, \(t) target %in% t))

mean(labeled$y)

[1] 0.181339




target <- "Student activities" names the topic we will predict. Change it to try another.

map_lgl(topics, \(t) target %in% t) goes through each answer’s list of codes and asks “is the target one of them?”, returning TRUE or FALSE for each. (map_lgl is a function that applies a small function to each item and returns logical values. The \(t) ... is the small function: “given a list of codes t, check whether the target is in it.”)
The result is saved as a new column y. By tradition, y is the thing we want to predict, called the outcome or label.

mean(labeled$y) gives the share of TRUE values, which is the share of answers carrying this code.

About one answer in five carries this code. That imbalance matters for how we judge the model, as we will see.

7.4 Step 2: Split before you do anything else
We will hold back 20% of the data to test the model. Two rules:


Split first. Anything the model “learns” from the test set, even the vocabulary, makes the test score optimistic. This is called data leakage.

Split by student, not by answer. One student can have a strength answer and a concern answer. If one lands in training and the other in testing, the model has effectively seen the student. Splitting by resp_id keeps each student on one side.


set.seed(664)
students <- unique(labeled$resp_id)
test_students <- sample(students, size = round(0.2 * length(students)))

train <- labeled |> filter(!resp_id %in% test_students)
test  <- labeled |> filter( resp_id %in% test_students)

c(train = nrow(train), test = nrow(test))

train  test 
 1529   368 




set.seed(664) makes the random split reproducible (see Appendix A).

unique(labeled$resp_id) lists each student once.

sample(students, size = ...) picks a random set of students. round(0.2 * length(students)) is 20% of them.
The last two lines build the two tables: train has answers from students not in the test set (!resp_id %in% test_students), and test has answers from students who are.

c(train = ..., test = ...) prints the two sizes side by side.

text:
7.6 Step 4: Fit a regularized logistic regression
Now the model itself. We use logistic regression, a standard method for predicting a yes/no outcome. It produces, for each answer, a probability that the answer carries the code (for instance, 0.83 means “83% likely”). It does so by giving each word a coefficient: a number saying how strongly that word pushes the prediction toward “yes” (positive) or “no” (negative).
The problem is that we have hundreds of words and only a modest number of answers. A plain regression would latch onto every quirk of the training data, which is called overfitting. The fix is regularization: adding a penalty on the size of the coefficients, so the model only keeps a word if it earns its place. We use the lasso, a kind of regularization that pushes most coefficients all the way to zero. The result is a short list of words that matter, which is easy to read.

set.seed(664)
fit <- cv.glmnet(x_train, train$y, family = "binomial",
                 alpha = 1, type.measure = "auc")

fit$lambda.1se

[1] 0.01971828

sum(coef(fit, s = "lambda.1se")[-1] != 0)   # words with a nonzero coefficient

[1] 19


cv.glmnet() fits the model. The options that matter:






Option
What it means



x_train
The matrix of word scores (the features)


train$y
The yes/no outcome to learn


family = "binomial"
“The outcome is yes/no,” which makes this logistic regression


alpha = 1
Use the lasso penalty. (Setting it to 0 gives a different penalty, called ridge, that shrinks coefficients but does not zero them out. Values in between mix the two)


type.measure = "auc"
The score used to choose the penalty strength. AUC is explained shortly



How strong should the penalty be? The strength is called lambda. Too small and the model overfits; too large and it ignores everything. cv.glmnet() finds a good value using cross-validation: it splits the training data into pieces, repeatedly trains on most of the pieces and tests on the one left out, and averages the results across many lambda values. (The test data we set aside is never touched during this.)


fit$lambda.1se prints the chosen penalty strength. It is the largest penalty whose score is within one standard error of the best, which gives a simpler model that usually generalizes about as well as the single best one. (The alternative, fit$lambda.min, picks the single best.)
The last line counts the words with a non-zero coefficient, the words the lasso kept. coef(fit, s = "lambda.1se") extracts the coefficients; [-1] drops the first one (the intercept, a baseline that is not a word); != 0 asks which are not zero; and sum() counts the TRUEs.

7.7 Step 5: Judge it on data it has not seen

test$p <- as.numeric(predict(fit, x_test, s = "lambda.1se", type = "response"))

head(test |> select(text, y, p), 6)

# A tibble: 6 × 3
  text                                                               y         p
  <chr>                                                              <lgl> <dbl>
1 getting help when needed, which made my first year easier. The li… TRUE  0.172
2 Barriers around study space renovations. I'd gladly help if someo… FALSE 0.111
3 Enjoyed the support for students                                   FALSE 0.111
4 Confusing chances to give feedback                                 FALSE 0.111
5 financial aid paperwork                                            FALSE 0.111
6 The people - needs attention, more support with wait times for th… FALSE 0.111


predict() applies the fitted model to new data. We give it the test matrix (x_test), the penalty to use (s = "lambda.1se"), and type = "response", which asks for probabilities instead of raw scores. as.numeric() converts the result to a plain list of numbers, and we store it as a new column p in the test table. The last line shows six answers with the true label y and the model’s probability p.
Each answer gets a predicted probability. To turn it into a yes/no call, pick a threshold: calls above it are “yes,” the rest “no.” Start at 0.5, and note that this is a choice.

metrics <- function(truth, p, threshold = 0.5) {
  pred <- p >= threshold
  tp <- sum(pred & truth); fp <- sum(pred & !truth)
  fn <- sum(!pred & truth); tn <- sum(!pred & !truth)
  precision <- if (tp + fp > 0) tp / (tp + fp) else NA_real_
  recall    <- tp / (tp + fn)
  tibble(tp, fp, fn, tn,
         accuracy  = (tp + tn) / length(truth),
         precision, recall,
         f1 = 2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall))
}

# Area under the ROC curve: the chance a random positive outranks a random negative
auc <- function(truth, p) {
  r <- rank(p)
  n1 <- sum(truth); n0 <- sum(!truth)
  (sum(r[truth]) - n1 * (n1 + 1) / 2) / (n1 * n0)
}

metrics(test$y, test$p)

# A tibble: 1 × 8
     tp    fp    fn    tn accuracy precision recall    f1
  <int> <int> <int> <int>    <dbl>     <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>
1    22     2    53   291    0.851     0.917  0.293 0.444

auc(test$y, test$p)

[1] 0.7811604


These are two more functions we wrote ourselves. metrics() takes the true answers (truth), the model’s probabilities (p), and a threshold (with a default of 0.5, written threshold = 0.5, so you can leave it out), and counts four kinds of outcome:








Model says YES
Model says NO



Truly yes

tp (true positive: correct hit)

fn (false negative: a miss)


Truly no

fp (false positive: false alarm)

tn (true negative: correct rejection)



This 2×2 grid is called a confusion matrix. Everything below is calculated from its four cells. pred <- p >= threshold makes the yes/no calls, and each sum(pred & truth) counts the answers where both are TRUE, and so on. (The & means “and.”)
Read the output before the definitions. At a threshold of 0.5 the model is cautious: when it says “Student activities” it is nearly always right (high precision), but it says so rarely and misses most of the real ones (low recall). The AUC of about 0.8 says the probabilities do carry useful signal; the 0.5 cutoff is just not the best place to draw the line.
Five numbers deserve plain definitions:


Accuracy: the share of all calls that were right, (tp + tn) / total.

Precision: of the answers the model called “Student activities,” the share that really are. tp / (tp + fp). It answers “when it says yes, can I trust it?”

Recall: of the answers that really are “Student activities,” the share the model found. tp / (tp + fn). It answers “how many of the real ones did it catch?”

F1: a single number that balances precision and recall (it is their harmonic mean, which is low whenever either one is low).

AUC (area under the curve): how well the model ranks answers, regardless of any threshold. It equals the chance that a randomly chosen “yes” answer gets a higher probability than a randomly chosen “no” answer. 0.5 means guessing; 1.0 means perfect ranking. The auc() function computes it from the ranks of the predictions.


7.7.1 Accuracy alone is misleading
A model that says “no” to every answer gets an accuracy equal to the share of “no” answers:

1 - mean(test$y)

[1] 0.7961957


That is the bar to beat. Our model’s accuracy is only a few points above it, even though the model is clearly doing something useful, which is why accuracy is a poor yardstick when one class is rare. Precision, recall, and AUC tell you much more.

7.7.2 The threshold is a dial
Lowering the threshold finds more true answers (recall rises) but also flags more wrong ones (precision falls).

map_dfr(seq(0.05, 0.8, by = 0.05),
        \(th) metrics(test$y, test$p, th) |> mutate(threshold = th)) |>
  select(threshold, precision, recall, f1) |>
  pivot_longer(-threshold) |>
  ggplot(aes(threshold, value, color = name)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(f1 = vcu_dark, precision = vcu_teal, recall = vcu_gold)) +
  labs(x = "Threshold", y = NULL, color = NULL)






Figure 7.2: Precision, recall, and F1 as the threshold changes.






seq(0.05, 0.8, by = 0.05) makes a list of thresholds from 0.05 to 0.8 in steps of 0.05.

map_dfr(..., \(th) metrics(...)) runs our metrics() function once for each threshold and stacks the results into one table, adding a threshold column.

pivot_longer(-threshold) reshapes the table (the reverse of pivot_wider): the columns for precision, recall, and F1 are gathered into one name column and one value column, which is the shape ggplot needs to draw three lines. The -threshold means “everything except this column.”

color = name draws a separate colored line for each measure.

Which threshold is right depends on the job. If a human will review every flagged answer, favor recall: you do not want to miss any. If the model’s calls go straight into a report, favor precision.

text:
7.8 Step 6: What did it learn?
The lasso gives us a readable answer. The words with the largest positive coefficients push toward “Student activities”; the most negative push away.

coefs <- coef(fit, s = "lambda.1se")
coef_df <- tibble(word = rownames(coefs), beta = as.numeric(coefs)) |>
  filter(word != "(Intercept)", beta != 0)

coef_df |>
  slice_max(abs(beta), n = 24) |>
  ggplot(aes(beta, reorder(word, beta), fill = beta > 0)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = vcu_teal, `FALSE` = vcu_gold)) +
  labs(x = "Coefficient (log-odds)", y = NULL)






Figure 7.3: Words most associated with the Student activities code.




The first part pulls the coefficients into a table with one row per word, dropping the intercept and any word whose coefficient the lasso set to zero. The chart keeps the 24 words with the largest coefficients in either direction (abs() takes the absolute value, ignoring sign) and colors each bar by whether it is positive (teal) or negative (gold) (fill = beta > 0).
The units are log-odds. You do not need to interpret them precisely: a positive number means the word makes “yes” more likely, a negative one makes it less likely, and a bigger number is a stronger push.
Do these words make sense for the topic? If you see “events,” “clubs,” and “organizations” pushing up, the model learned something real. If you see odd words, such as the name of one interviewer’s favorite example, it is learning quirks of the data, and you should be skeptical.

text:
7.9 Step 7: Read the mistakes
The most useful thing you can do with a classifier is read where it is wrong.

# Missed: coded as the topic, but given the lowest probabilities
test |>
  filter(y) |>
  arrange(p) |>
  slice_head(n = 6) |>
  select(p, text)

# A tibble: 6 × 2
      p text                                                                    
  <dbl> <chr>                                                                   
1 0.111 teaching assistants                                                     
2 0.111 Solid system. Good graduation checks.                                   
3 0.111 How things are run - they really try                                    
4 0.111 consistency between offices                                             
5 0.111 Compared to other schools, the support for students are ahead, thankful…
6 0.111 Too expensive: the overall experience. Problems with the chances to giv…

# False alarms: not coded as the topic, but given the highest probabilities
test |>
  filter(!y) |>
  arrange(desc(p)) |>
  slice_head(n = 6) |>
  select(p, text)

# A tibble: 6 × 2
      p text                                                                    
  <dbl> <chr>                                                                   
1 0.718 networking events - very helpful                                        
2 0.545 The networking events kept me on track.                                 
3 0.358 The opportunities here here are strong and I appreciate the capstone pr…
4 0.313 I'd say the networking events stands out. My roommate had the opposite …
5 0.299 Love the campus in general.                                             
6 0.248 Love the system. Easy to use: the networking events, i appreciate the c…


The first block takes the answers that were coded with the topic (filter(y)), sorts them by the model’s probability from lowest to highest (arrange(p)), and shows the first six: the ones the model was most sure were not the topic. The second block does the reverse: answers that were not coded (filter(!y)), sorted from highest probability down (arrange(desc(p))): the ones the model was most sure were the topic.
Mistakes usually fall into three bins. Some are real model failures: the answer is clearly about activities, and the model missed it, often because it uses a word the training data never saw. Some are label noise: the answer is not really about activities, and the interviewer ticked the box anyway, or the reverse. And some are judgment calls that two human coders would disagree about. If many errors are the second and third kind, the model’s ceiling is limited by the labels, not by the algorithm.
The lists above show examples of each. Among the missed answers, several barely mention the topic they were coded with: the code is there, but the words are not. That is label noise, and the model cannot be blamed for failing to find words that are not in the text. Among the false alarms, many are about networking and professional events, which are near the Student activities topic but were coded under professional development instead. Whether they belong is a coding-scheme question that no algorithm can settle.

text:
7.10 Step 8: Scaling up to many topics
The same recipe works for any topic. We wrap it in a function and run it for the topics with enough examples. Because we reuse the vocabulary and the split, the comparison across topics is fair.

fit_topic <- function(topic) {
  y_tr <- map_lgl(train$topics, \(t) topic %in% t)
  y_te <- map_lgl(test$topics,  \(t) topic %in% t)

  set.seed(664)
  f <- cv.glmnet(x_train, y_tr, family = "binomial", alpha = 1, type.measure = "auc")
  p <- as.numeric(predict(f, x_test, s = "lambda.1se", type = "response"))

  # Use each topic's own base rate as a data-driven threshold
  th <- mean(y_tr)
  bind_cols(
    tibble(topic = topic, prevalence = mean(y_te), auc = auc(y_te, p)),
    metrics(y_te, p, threshold = th) |> select(precision, recall, f1)
  )
}

common_topics <- topic_counts |> filter(n >= 80) |> pull(topics)
common_topics <- setdiff(common_topics, "Other")

results <- map_dfr(common_topics, fit_topic) |> arrange(desc(auc))

fit_topic() is a third function of our own. Given a topic name, it repeats everything we just did: builds the yes/no outcome for that topic in the training and test sets, fits the lasso, predicts for the test set, and returns one row of results (the topic, how common it is, AUC, precision, recall, and F1). A few details:

For the threshold, it uses each topic’s own base rate in the training data (th <- mean(y_tr)). That is a rough and reasonable choice, because rare topics need a lower bar than common ones. (At 0.5, rare topics would almost never be flagged.)

bind_cols() joins two small tables side by side.

After defining it, we select the topics worth modeling: those with at least 80 labeled answers (filter(n >= 80)), excluding the catch-all “Other” (setdiff() removes items from a list). map_dfr(common_topics, fit_topic) then runs fit_topic() for each, stacking the rows, and arrange(desc(auc)) sorts the best-predicted topic to the top. The last line rounds all the number columns to two decimals (across(where(is.numeric), ...) means “every column that holds numbers”).

ggplot(results, aes(auc, reorder(topic, auc))) +
  geom_point(size = 3, color = vcu_teal) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed") +
  xlim(0.45, 1) +
  labs(x = "AUC on held-out students", y = NULL)






Figure 7.4: Test-set AUC for each topic. The dashed line is chance.




This plots each topic’s AUC as a dot. The dashed line at 0.5 marks chance; dots to its right mean the model beats guessing. (xlim(0.45, 1) sets the horizontal range.)
In this synthetic data, how well a topic is predicted mostly reflects how many examples it has and how much noise was built in, not how abstract the topic is. With real interviews you would expect a wider spread: concrete topics such as housing or financial aid tend to be easy, because students use distinctive words for them, while abstract topics such as “sense of belonging” tend to be harder, because students express them in many different ways. When that happens, a topic’s difficulty tells you something about the topic as much as about the model.
Two cautions on reading this table. First, each topic is scored on a single test split with only 20 to 75 true cases, so differences of a few hundredths in AUC are noise. Second, you may see a glmnet convergence warning on some topics. It means the optimizer did not finish for the very smallest penalties on a weak-signal topic, and glmnet returns the solutions for the larger penalties instead. It is worth knowing about but does not invalidate the table.

Unsupervised (Ch. 3-6)

title: 7  Supervised Learning: Predicting Topic Codes
text:
7.12 Summary

A supervised model learns from labeled training data and is graded on held-out test data.
Split first, by student, and build the vocabulary from training data only, to avoid data leakage.
A lasso on TF-IDF gives a strong, interpretable baseline: most words get a coefficient of zero, and the rest show what drives the prediction.
Judge with precision, recall, and AUC, not accuracy, when classes are imbalanced. The threshold is a dial that trades one against the other.
Read the errors. They tell you whether to improve the model or the labels.

title: 8  Embeddings: Using a Pretrained Language Model
text:
8.1 What is an embedding?
Data for this chapter: data/vcu_cares_long.csv and data/embeddings_minilm.csv, the latter built by py/embed.py
In Chapter 7 we taught a model to predict the interviewers’ topic codes from word counts. That worked reasonably well, but it has a built-in weakness: to a word-count model, “advisor” and “counselor” are as unrelated as “advisor” and “parking.” It only knows about the exact words it saw in training.
A pretrained language model has already read an enormous amount of text, and from it has learned which words and phrases are used in similar ways. We can borrow that knowledge. This chapter shows how to turn each answer into a list of numbers that captures its meaning, and then to use those numbers in the same lasso model as before.
By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain what an embedding is, create embeddings with a small model that runs on your own computer, use them to predict topic codes, and judge when they help and when they do not.
An embedding is a list of numbers that represents a piece of text. You can think of it as the text’s address in a map of meaning. Texts that mean similar things get addresses that are close together, and texts that mean different things get addresses far apart.
A map of a city needs two numbers (latitude and longitude) to place a building. A map of meaning needs many more, because meaning has many dimensions. The model we use, MiniLM, uses 384 numbers for every answer. No single number has a human-readable meaning (there is no “advising dimension”). What matters is the pattern across all 384, and how close two patterns are.
A few terms you will see:
crumbs: 8  Embeddings: Using a Pretrained Language Model

title: 8  Embeddings: Using a Pretrained Language Model
text:
Vector: just a list of numbers. An answer’s embedding is a vector of length 384.

Dimension: one position in that list. We say the embeddings have 384 dimensions.

Cosine similarity: a score for how close two vectors point in the same direction, from -1 to 1. High means similar meaning. When vectors have been scaled to length 1, as ours are, cosine similarity is just the dot product: multiply the numbers position by position and add them up.
crumbs: 8  Embeddings: Using a Pretrained Language Model

title: 8  Embeddings: Using a Pretrained Language Model
text:
8.2 Why this might help
Recall the limits of word counts from earlier chapters. Two answers can describe the same thing in different words (“my advisor was helpful” and “the counselor really supported me”), and a word-count model sees little in common. An embedding places both answers close together, because the pretrained model learned that these words appear in similar contexts.
This should matter most when you have few labeled examples. A word-count model must learn from scratch that “advisor,” “counselor,” and “mentor” all point toward the same topic, which takes many examples. An embedding already contains that knowledge, so the lasso may be able to learn the topic from fewer examples. Learning from a small number of labeled examples is called few-shot learning, and we test the idea directly below. (It turns out to be partly true.)
crumbs: 8  Embeddings: Using a Pretrained Language Model

title: 8  Embeddings: Using a Pretrained Language Model
text:
8.3 About the model
MiniLM (all-MiniLM-L6-v2) is a small transformer, the kind of neural network behind modern language models. It has about 22 million adjustable parameters, which is tiny by today’s standards (the chat-style language models you may have heard of have thousands of times more). That is why it is a good teaching choice:

It is small: about 90 MB to download.
It is fast: embedding all of our answers takes about a minute on an ordinary computer, with no special graphics hardware.
It runs locally. Nothing is sent to a company’s server, and no account, key, or fee is involved.







ImportantYour text stays on your computer



The only network step is the first-time download of the model files, which contain no data about your answers. After that the model works offline. This is a major difference from using a hosted chat service, where every answer would be sent to an outside company. If you work with real student responses, running a model locally keeps the text where it belongs. (Check that your own approvals cover using a model to code the data at all, which is a separate question.)

title: 8  Embeddings: Using a Pretrained Language Model
text:
8.4 Step 1: Create the embeddings
Embedding is done in a short Python script, because the pretrained models are distributed in Python. You run it once, and it saves a file that the rest of the chapter reads in R. This is the only Python in the book.
"""Turn every answer into a list of 384 numbers (an "embedding") with a small
pretrained language model, and save them for use in R.

Run from the project root, after  Rscript R/01-prep-data.R :

    python py/embed.py

Input : data/vcu_cares_long.csv        (one row per answer; built by the prep script)
Output: data/embeddings_minilm.csv     (doc_id plus 384 columns, e1 ... e384)

The model runs on your own computer. No text is sent anywhere. The only
network step is the first-time download of the model files (about 90 MB), which
contain no data; after that it works offline.
"""
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import pandas as pd
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

MODEL_NAME = "sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2"
MODEL_REVISION = "1110a243fdf4706b3f48f1d95db1a4f5529b4d41"   # exact model version used for this book; set to None to use the latest
IN_PATH = Path("data/vcu_cares_long.csv")
OUT_PATH = Path("data/embeddings_minilm.csv")


def main():
    if not IN_PATH.exists():
        sys.exit(f"Can't find {IN_PATH}. Run  Rscript R/01-prep-data.R  from the project root first.")

    # keep_default_na=False so that an answer that is literally the text "NA" stays text
    answers = pd.read_csv(IN_PATH, usecols=["doc_id", "text"], keep_default_na=False)

    # Same apostrophe clean-up that load_vcu() does in R, so both sides see the same text
    texts = answers["text"].str.replace("[‘’]", "'", regex=True).tolist()

    model = SentenceTransformer(MODEL_NAME, revision=MODEL_REVISION)

    # Print the exact model version (a "commit hash") so it can be recorded or pinned
    try:
        from huggingface_hub import model_info
        print("Model:", MODEL_NAME, "| revision:", MODEL_REVISION or model_info(MODEL_NAME).sha)
    except Exception:
        print("Model:", MODEL_NAME, "| revision: (could not look up)")

    # normalize_embeddings=True rescales each vector to length 1, which makes the
    # dot product of two answers equal to their cosine similarity
    vectors = model.encode(texts, batch_size=64, normalize_embeddings=True, show_progress_bar=False)

    out = pd.DataFrame(vectors, columns=[f"e{i + 1}" for i in range(vectors.shape[1])])
    out.insert(0, "doc_id", answers["doc_id"].to_numpy())
    OUT_PATH.parent.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    out.to_csv(OUT_PATH, index=False, float_format="%.6g")
    print(f"Wrote {len(out)} embeddings of length {vectors.shape[1]} to {OUT_PATH}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
Here is what the script does.


Reads the answers from the long file the prep script made (pd.read_csv). It keeps only two columns, the answer’s ID and its text.

Straightens curly apostrophes, exactly as load_vcu() does in R, so that both sides see the same text.

Loads the model (SentenceTransformer(MODEL_NAME, revision = MODEL_REVISION)). The first time, this downloads the model files and stores them on your computer. The script names the exact model version to use (MODEL_REVISION, a “commit hash”), which freezes it so that a later update to the model cannot silently change your results. If you want to try the newest version, set MODEL_REVISION to None; the script prints the version it used either way, so you can record it.

Encodes every answer (model.encode(...)). batch_size = 64 processes 64 answers at a time, which is faster than one by one. normalize_embeddings = True rescales each vector to length 1, which is what lets a dot product act as cosine similarity.

Saves a table with one row per answer: its doc_id and 384 columns named e1 to e384.

To run it, install the Python packages once (see SETUP.md), and then, from the project folder:
python py/embed.py

       call. = FALSE)
}
emb <- read_csv("data/embeddings_minilm.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

dim(emb)

[1] 3614  385




source("R/classification.R") loads the functions from Chapter 7 (building the TF-IDF features, the lasso, AUC) so that we can reuse them. They are the same functions, saved in a file.

read_csv() reads the embeddings. The result has one row per answer and 385 columns: doc_id plus the 384 numbers.


8.5.1 A look at “closeness”
To see what the numbers capture, pick an answer and find the five answers whose embeddings are closest to it.

# Look up each answer's embedding by its ID, and keep the numbers as a matrix
embed_matrix <- function(d) as.matrix(emb[match(d$doc_id, emb$doc_id), -1])
e_all <- embed_matrix(vcu)

set.seed(664)
i <- sample(nrow(vcu), 1)

# With length-1 vectors, the dot product is the cosine similarity
similarity <- as.numeric(e_all %*% e_all[i, ])

closest <- tibble(text = vcu$text, similarity = similarity) |>
  slice(-i) |>
  slice_max(similarity, n = 5, with_ties = FALSE)

# the chosen answer first (similarity 1 with itself), then its five closest neighbors
bind_rows(tibble(text = vcu$text[i], similarity = 1), closest)

# A tibble: 6 × 2
  text                                                                similarity
  <chr>                                                                    <dbl>
1 expand communication, give students a say in the aid refund timing…      1    
2 add more opportunities here. Fund the support for students. Fund t…      0.744
3 1. give students a say in the financial aid paperwork 2. expand re…      0.741
4 make resources available free. Extend hours for the aid refund tim…      0.731
5 Make resources available free. Improve the support for students. E…      0.730
6 Make course workload free, Hire more people for the communication.…      0.715




embed_matrix() is a small function of ours: for any set of answers it looks up their rows in the embedding table and returns just the numbers as a matrix. match() finds each answer’s row by its ID.

sample(nrow(vcu), 1) picks one answer at random (set.seed() makes it the same one each time), and i is its position.

e_all %*% e_all[i, ] is the key line. The %*% symbol means matrix multiplication; here it takes the dot product of every answer’s vector with the chosen answer’s vector, which gives a similarity score for all answers at once.

slice(-i) drops the chosen answer itself from the candidates, and slice_max() keeps the five with the highest similarity. The last line puts the chosen answer on top (similarity 1, by definition, with itself), followed by its five closest neighbors, most similar first.

Read the neighbors. They should be answers that talk about the same kind of thing. This is the idea behind the whole chapter: closeness in the embedding space tracks closeness in meaning, so a model that learns from the embeddings can generalize across different wordings.

8.6 Step 3: The same task, with embeddings
We now predict the topic codes exactly as in Chapter 7, with the same train and test students (the helper function uses the same seed), but with embeddings as the features in place of TF-IDF.

labeled <- make_labeled(vcu)
sp      <- split_by_student(labeled)
train   <- sp$train
test    <- sp$test

c(train = nrow(train), test = nrow(test))

train  test 
 1529   368 

# Features, two ways
tf      <- tfidf_features(train, test)     # word-count features (Chapter 7)
e_train <- embed_matrix(train)             # embedding features
e_test  <- embed_matrix(test)



make_labeled() and split_by_student() repeat the first two steps of Chapter 7: keep the answers that have topic codes, then hold out 20% of students for testing. Because the seed is the same, the train and test sets are identical to those in the last chapter.

tfidf_features() builds the word-count (TF-IDF) matrices, as before.

embed_matrix() builds the embedding matrices for the same answers.

Now the target from before, “Student activities”:

target <- "Student activities"
y_train <- has_topic(train, target)
y_test  <- has_topic(test,  target)

# lambda.min.ratio and nlambda shorten the penalty path (explained below)
p_tfidf <- lasso_probs(tf$x_train, y_train, tf$x_test)
p_embed <- lasso_probs(e_train,    y_train, e_test, lambda.min.ratio = 0.01, nlambda = 50)

tibble(features = c("TF-IDF (word counts)", "MiniLM embeddings"),
       auc = c(auc(y_test, p_tfidf), auc(y_test, p_embed)))

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  features               auc
  <chr>                <dbl>
1 TF-IDF (word counts) 0.781
2 MiniLM embeddings    0.768




has_topic() is another helper: for each answer it says whether the target topic is among its codes (TRUE or FALSE).

lasso_probs() fits the lasso on the training answers and returns the predicted probability for each test answer. It is the same cv.glmnet() fit as in Chapter 7, wrapped in a function. We call it once with each kind of features.

auc() scores each set of predictions. AUC is 0.5 for guessing and 1.0 for perfect ranking (see Chapter 7).

The TF-IDF number is the same one you saw in Chapter 7, which is a good check that we are comparing like with like. For this topic the embeddings scored 0.77 against 0.78 for word counts, so they did slightly worse. One topic can be a fluke, which is why we look at all of them next.






NoteWhy the embedding fit has two extra options



lambda.min.ratio = 0.01 and nlambda = 50 tell cv.glmnet() to try fewer, and larger, penalty values. With 384 dense columns the default search over very small penalties is slow and rarely changes the answer: in our tests it gave essentially the same AUC about ten times faster. The TF-IDF fit keeps the defaults so that it matches Chapter 7.

One topic can be a fluke. Here is the comparison for every topic with enough examples.

                                            lambda.min.ratio = 0.01, nlambda = 50)))

8.7 Step 4: How many labeled examples do you need?
The claim in the introduction was that embeddings help most when labeled examples are scarce. We can test that directly with a learning curve: train on smaller and smaller samples of the training answers, and see how the score changes.

learning_curve <- function(topic, sizes, reps = 4) {
  y_all <- has_topic(train, topic)
  y_te  <- has_topic(test,  topic)

  # every size is repeated reps times with different random samples (the full set once)
  grid <- expand.grid(n = sizes, rep = seq_len(reps)) |>
    filter(!(n >= nrow(train) & rep > 1))

  pmap_dfr(grid, \(n, rep) {
    set.seed(1000 * rep + n)
    idx <- if (n >= nrow(train)) seq_len(nrow(train)) else sample(nrow(train), n)
    y <- y_all[idx]
    if (sum(y) < 5 || sum(!y) < 5) return(tibble())   # too few examples of one kind to fit

    tfi <- tfidf_features(train[idx, ], test)
    tibble(topic = topic, n = n, rep = rep,
           tfidf      = suppressWarnings(auc(y_te, lasso_probs(tfi$x_train, y, tfi$x_test))),
           embeddings = suppressWarnings(auc(y_te, lasso_probs(e_train[idx, ], y, e_test,
                                                              lambda.min.ratio = 0.01, nlambda = 50))))
  })
}

sizes  <- c(40, 80, 160, 320, 640, nrow(train))
topics <- c("Student activities", "Student support services", "Having a sense of belonging")

curve <- map_dfr(topics, learning_curve, sizes = sizes) |>
  pivot_longer(c(tfidf, embeddings), names_to = "features", values_to = "auc")

curve |>
  group_by(features, n) |>
  summarise(mean_auc = round(mean(auc, na.rm = TRUE), 3), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = features, values_from = mean_auc)

# A tibble: 6 × 3
      n embeddings tfidf
  <dbl>      <dbl> <dbl>
1    40      0.529 0.5  
2    80      0.536 0.5  
3   160      0.693 0.617
4   320      0.727 0.668
5   640      0.768 0.776
6  1529      0.808 0.803


How this works:


learning_curve() is a function of ours. For a given topic, it draws a random sample of n training answers, fits both models on just that sample, and scores them on the same test set every time. It does this at several sample sizes, and repeats each size four times with different random samples (reps = 4), because a single small sample can be unrepresentative.

if (sum(y) < 5 || sum(!y) < 5) return(tibble()) skips a sample that contains fewer than five examples of “yes” or of “no”: the model cannot learn from nothing.
We run it for three common topics, then stack the results and pivot them into a table of average AUC at each size.


curve_mean <- curve |>
  group_by(features, n) |>
  summarise(auc = mean(auc, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

ggplot() +
  geom_line(data = curve |> group_by(topic, features, n) |> summarise(auc = mean(auc, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop"),
            aes(n, auc, color = features, group = interaction(topic, features)),
            linewidth = 0.4, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_line(data = curve_mean, aes(n, auc, color = features), linewidth = 1.4) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(40, 80, 160, 320, 640, 1500)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(tfidf = vcu_gold, embeddings = vcu_teal)) +
  labs(x = "Labeled training answers (log scale)", y = "AUC on held-out students", color = NULL)






Figure 8.2: Test-set AUC as the number of labeled training answers grows. Thin lines are individual topics; thick lines are the average.




The horizontal axis is the number of labeled training answers, on a log scale (each tick is roughly double the last). The vertical axis is test AUC; the dashed line at 0.5 is chance. Each thin line is one topic, and the thick line is the average across topics. The embeddings are teal and the word counts are gold.

title: 8  Embeddings: Using a Pretrained Language Model
text:
8.8 What the results show
Here is what the comparison told us in our run. The numbers below are computed from the tables above.

8.8.1 With all the training data, embeddings did not win
Embeddings scored higher than word counts on 4 of the 12 topics, and on average were 0.02 AUC lower. Most of the differences are small, under about 0.04. Treat those as ties: each topic’s AUC comes from a single split of students with only 20 to 75 true cases, so gaps of a few hundredths are within noise.
The two largest gaps both favor word counts: Student professional development by 0.11 AUC and Health support by 0.09. Gaps that large may be real. A plausible reason is that those topics are signaled by distinctive words that word counts catch directly, but we have not tested that.

8.8.2 With a few hundred labeled answers, they helped
The learning curve is where embeddings earned their keep, though not at the smallest sizes.


Below about 100 answers, neither learned much. With 40 and 80 answers the embeddings averaged 0.53 and 0.54 (barely above the 0.5 chance line), and word counts sat at exactly 0.5. The word-count figure is partly an artifact of our rule that a word must appear in at least five training answers, which leaves almost no vocabulary to work with when you have 40 answers. It is not a hard limit of word counts.

From about 150 to 300 answers, embeddings led. At 160 answers they were ahead by about 0.08 AUC, and at 320 by about 0.06.

By about 640 answers the advantage was gone, and with all 1,529 training answers the two were essentially tied (0.81 against 0.80).

So the few-shot idea is partly supported. Embeddings helped most in the middle range of a few hundred labeled answers, which happens to be a realistic number for a lab to code by hand. They did not rescue us when almost no labels were available, and they gave no advantage once labels were plentiful. Remember that this is an average over three topics and four random samples per size, so the exact numbers will wiggle if you change the seed.






WarningWhat synthetic data can and cannot show here



The text in this book’s data was generated from short phrase templates, so it is unusually clean and repetitive. That is the setting where simple word counts do well, because the same words really do signal the same topic, and it leaves little for an embedding to add. That fits what we saw: a tie overall, with an edge only in the middle of the learning curve. Real interview answers are messier: students say the same thing in many different ways, which is exactly where embeddings are expected to pull ahead. So do not conclude from our numbers that embeddings do not help. They show you how to run the comparison and read it; the comparison on real data is the one that matters.
There is also a ceiling that no model can pass. Some of the interviewers’ codes are not reflected in the words of the answer, which is label noise (see Chapter 7). A better model cannot find signal that is not there.

8.9 Choosing between the two








TF-IDF + lasso
Embeddings + lasso



Setup
R only
Adds one Python step and a model download


Speed
Very fast
Slower to prepare (embedding), then similar


Labeled examples needed
Struggled below a few hundred
Led at 150 to 300 in our run; neither learned much below about 100


Handles different wording
Poorly (“advisor” and “counselor” look unrelated)
Better in principle. Our clean synthetic text does not really test this


Can you read why it predicts a topic?
Yes: the lasso keeps named words
No: the 384 numbers have no names



The last row is a real cost. With word counts, the lasso hands you a list of words (“events,” “clubs”) that you can read and check. With embeddings, the model’s reasons are spread over 384 unnamed numbers. When you must be able to explain and audit a prediction, that interpretability may be worth more than a small gain in accuracy.

title: 8  Embeddings: Using a Pretrained Language Model
text:
8.10 Summary

An embedding turns a text into a list of numbers so that similar meanings land close together. A pretrained model has learned this from huge amounts of text.

MiniLM is small enough to run on your own computer, with no account, fee, or data leaving the machine. It is created once with a short Python script, and the rest happens in R.
Using embeddings as features in the same lasso lets us compare directly with word counts, on the same held-out students.
In our run the two tied with all the training data. Embeddings led when there were a few hundred labeled answers, and neither learned much below about 100.
A learning curve shows how performance depends on the number of labeled examples, which is how you test the few-shot idea.
Embeddings cost interpretability, and on clean synthetic text their advantage is small. Run the comparison on your own data before choosing.

title: 9  Wrapping Up
text:
9.1 The same answers, seven ways
We used one dataset and seven methods. This chapter pulls them together: what each one is for, how to choose among them, how to describe what you did in writing, and where to go next. There is no new code here, only the thinking that should surround the code.
Each method looked at the same text and asked a different question.
A useful way to sort them is by how much you tell the computer in advance.
The more you tell it, the more you can check its work, and the more its answers reflect your choices.

title: 9  Wrapping Up
text:
Method
Question it answers
What you give it
What you get back




Word counts (Ch. 2)
What words come up most?
Text
Frequencies


TF-IDF (Ch. 3)
What words distinguish this group from others?
Text and groups
A distinctiveness score per word


LDA (Ch. 4)
What themes run through the text?
Text and K
Topics and per-document mixes


STM (Ch. 5)
What themes, and do they differ by group?
Text, K, covariates
Topics and effects with uncertainty


Lexicon sentiment (Ch. 6)
How positive or negative is the language?
Text and a lexicon
A score per document


Supervised classification (Ch. 7)
Can we reproduce a human coding?
Text and labels
A predictive model and its accuracy


Embeddings + classification (Ch. 8)
Does a pretrained model’s sense of meaning help, especially with few labels?
Text, labels, a pretrained model
A predictive model, often better with few examples





Descriptive methods (counts, TF-IDF) tell it nothing except how to split text into words. They summarize what is there.
Unsupervised methods (topic models) tell it how many themes to look for, and let it propose them. You decide what the themes mean.
Lexicon methods (sentiment) tell it what words mean, through a dictionary someone else built.
Supervised methods (classification) tell it the right answers for some examples, and ask it to generalize.
Pretrained models (embeddings) lend it knowledge learned from huge amounts of other text, so that it needs fewer examples from yours.

title: 9  Wrapping Up
text:
9.2 Choosing a method
Start from the question, not the technique.

“I want to get a feel for the data.” Counts and bigrams, then read.
“I want to compare two groups.” TF-IDF for a quick look, STM when you want estimates with uncertainty.
“I want themes but have no categories.” Topic models. Plan to spend your time reading and naming.
“I already have a coding scheme.” Supervised classification, to scale it up or to test whether it is learnable.
“I have a coding scheme but only a few coded examples, or people word things in many different ways.” Embeddings plus a simple classifier. Compare it with word counts on your own data with a learning curve, as in Chapter 8.
“I want to know how people feel.” Be careful. Lexicon scores measure vocabulary, and as we saw, concerns are worded with positive words. Consider a supervised model trained on human-rated examples.

title: 9  Wrapping Up
section: 9.3 Five habits that carried through the book
text:
9.3 Five habits that carried through the book

Decide what a document is. Every result depends on it. One answer, one student, and one question give different results.
Write your cleaning rules down. Stop words, placeholder answers, and vocabulary cutoffs are analytic choices. Someone should be able to see and change them.
Read the data. Before a method, to know what you are dealing with. After a method, to check what it found. Every chapter had a step where we went back to the original answers.
Distrust small groups. Intervals are wide, and rare words get inflated scores.
Separate “the method found it” from “it is true.” A topic is a pattern in word use. Whether it is a meaningful theme is a judgment.

title: 9  Wrapping Up
text:
9.4 Describing what you did
When you write up a text-mining analysis, readers cannot judge it unless they know the choices you made. A good methods paragraph covers the same things we decided along the way. Here is a template with the blanks filled in for an imagined analysis of these data.

We analyzed N answers from M students to three open-ended questions. Placeholder answers (e.g., “none,” “n/a”) were removed (k answers). Text was split into words, lowercased, and stripped of punctuation and numbers; we removed the Snowball stop-word list plus [list your domain stop words]. For topic modeling we combined each student’s answers into one document and retained words used by at least five students. We fit an LDA model with K topics (seed 664) and chose K by [how you chose it]. Two researchers independently named each topic from its highest-probability words and its five strongest documents; [how disagreements were resolved]. Analyses used R [version] with the tidytext and topicmodels packages.

The pieces to always include:







Report this
Why




How many documents, and what a “document” was
It shapes every result


Cleaning rules (stop words, removals)
They change which words matter


Settings (K, thresholds, seed, vocabulary cutoff)
So someone can reproduce your result


How topics were named and checked
Naming is a human judgment, not an output


For supervised models, the held-out performance, not the training performance
Training performance is always flattering


What the method cannot tell you
For example, that a topic is a pattern in words, not a verified theme

title: 9  Wrapping Up
section: 9.5 A checklist before you trust a result
text:
9.5 A checklist before you trust a result

Did I read a random sample of the raw text?
Do I know what a document is in this analysis?
Did I look at what my cleaning rules removed?
For a group comparison: how big are the groups, and are the differences larger than their error bars?
For topics: did I read the strongest documents for each, and would the topics survive a different seed or a different K?
For a classifier: was it tested on data it never saw, split by student?
For sentiment: did I check which words drive the score, and compare within a question?
Could someone else reproduce this from what I wrote down?

title: 9  Wrapping Up
text:
9.6 Working with student words
The book’s data are synthetic, but the real VCU CARES responses are students describing their lives, and you will work with data like that. A few practices follow:

Keep the raw data out of version control, as this project does, and carry only the variables you need.
Be careful quoting. A short, specific quote can identify someone even without a name, especially from a small program.
Report who is missing. These data over-represent undergraduates and people who came to events or were reached by interviewers. Say so.

title: 9  Wrapping Up
text:
9.7 Where to go next

Zero-shot learning. In Chapter 8 we still needed labeled examples to train the lasso. A zero-shot classifier needs none: you give it only the names of the topics, and it scores how well each answer fits each one. Compact models trained for this (natural-language-inference models) run locally, like MiniLM did.
Large language models for coding. A chat-style language model can apply a whole codebook to thousands of answers, with or without a few examples in the prompt (few-shot). Everything from Chapter 7 still applies: hold out human-coded answers and measure agreement before trusting it. One practical warning: most of these models are hosted services, which means every answer is sent to an outside company. For real student responses, check what your approvals allow, and consider models you can run on your own computer.
Inter-rater reliability. If two humans code the same answers, how often do they agree? That sets the ceiling for any classifier.
More reading. The references list two free online books, Text Mining with R and Supervised Machine Learning for Text Analysis in R, that go deeper on everything here.

The best next step is a project of your own. Bring a dataset to lab, decide what a document is, and start by reading.
If a term in this book was unfamiliar, Appendix B collects the key ones in one place, and Appendix A explains how to read the R code.

title: Appendix A — Reading R Code: A Short Guide
text:
A.1 Running code
You do not need to be a programmer to follow this book. You do need to be able to read the code, so you know what each block is doing before you run it. This appendix covers the handful of ideas that appear on almost every page. If a chapter’s code looks like a wall of symbols, come back here.
R code lives in two places in this book.
In RStudio, put the cursor on a line and press Ctrl+Enter (Cmd+Enter on a Mac) to run that line. Select several lines first to run them all. Output appears in the Console (text) or the Plots pane (charts). If you open a chapter (.qmd file), each gray block has a small green “play” button that runs the whole block.
Run blocks in order, from the top of the chapter. Later blocks use things that earlier blocks created, so skipping ahead is the most common reason for an error such as object 'vcu' not found.

text:
A.2 Comments
Anything after a # on a line is a comment: a note to the human reader that R ignores.

# This whole line is a comment
x <- 5   # and so is everything after the # on this line

Throughout the book we put short comments inside code to explain what a line is for.

title: Appendix A — Reading R Code: A Short Guide
text:
A.3 Objects and the arrow
R stores things under names. The arrow <- means “take what is on the right and save it under the name on the left.”

n_students <- 1241        # saves the number 1241 as n_students
greeting   <- "hello"     # saves a piece of text

Read <- aloud as “gets.” The thing you saved is called an object. Type its name on its own line to see what is inside it. Names are case-sensitive: vcu and VCU are different objects.

title: Appendix A — Reading R Code: A Short Guide
text:
A.4 Text, numbers, and TRUE/FALSE


Text (called a string or character value) goes in quotes: "hello". Single or double quotes both work.

Numbers have no quotes: 5, 3.14.

Logical values are TRUE or FALSE. They come from questions you ask of the data, such as n_words <= 3, which is TRUE for short answers and FALSE for the rest.

The comparison symbols you will see are:


Symbol
Means



==
is equal to (two equals signs; one = is something else)


!=
is not equal to



<, <=, >, >=

less than, at most, greater than, at least


!
not (flips TRUE and FALSE)


&
and


\|
or


%in%
is one of the values in this list
